lines: Same six rows of data, stored two different ways.
One of them is a single missed update away from telling you two different things at once.
Splitting data apart to kill redundancy sounds like it has to cost you a join somewhere down the line.
Does it always?
answer: It depends entirely on how the data actually gets queried afterward.
A handful of point lookups barely notice a join. A query that scans everything pays for it on every single row.

lines: Here is the actual rule underneath all of this.
One column determines another when every value on one side always comes with exactly the same value on the other.
Start from one column, and let every rule that already applies keep firing.
Each firing switches on more columns, until nothing new switches on at all.
That full set it eventually reaches is the whole point.
Whichever starting column gets you there, with nothing smaller able to do the same, is your real key.
Now here is a column that clearly determines something else on its own.
Does that earn it the same status?
answer: No, and the reason is mechanical, not a matter of opinion.
Its own reach stalls out early. It never gets anywhere near two of the other columns no matter how long you let it run.

lines: Trace it yourself and you will watch it stall in exactly the same place every time.
Determining one neighbor is not the same thing as determining the whole row.
Climb the first three rungs of this ladder and each one is answering a different complaint.
Keep every value a single thing, then make sure nothing depends on only part of a key, then cut anything depending on a non-key column instead of the key itself.
There is a gap the third rung quietly leaves open, and the next rung closes it.
Every single determining column now has to be a full key in its own right, not just determine something.
Up to here, every rule has been about one value picking out exactly one other value.
This next kind of rule is different: one value can pick out a whole independent set of others.
Split a table along one of these real rules, and something important is guaranteed.
Join the pieces back, and you get every original row back, exactly, with nothing lost and nothing invented.
That guarantee is not the only one worth keeping, and it is not automatic that you keep both.
You can satisfy it completely and still lose the ability to check an original rule without stitching things back together first.
Watch what actually happens when the same change gets made two different ways.
One version needs a single touch. The other needs several, and skipping just one of them leaves two conflicting answers sitting on file at the same time.
None of that makes storing it the second way a mistake by itself.
A workload built around scanning everything pays a real cost on every row for a join the other version never needed, so trading some risk for speed can be exactly the right call.
One determining rule, one full reach, one real key. Four rungs, each closing a gap the last one left open.
One guarantee you never skip, and one you sometimes trade away on purpose for speed.
Here is a new rule: one column determines every other column directly, with nothing else determining anything.
So what has to be the key?
answer: That one column, on its own.
Its reach already covers everything in a single step, and nothing smaller could possibly do the same job.
